deepDive.title: Limiting factors — why plants stop growing even when watered
deepDive.body: In Class 7 you learned that photosynthesis needs FOUR things: sunlight, chlorophyll, CO₂, and water. Class 8 introduces an important twist: at any moment, only ONE of these four is the bottleneck — and that's what controls the rate. Give a plant infinite water + sunlight, but starve it of CO₂, and photosynthesis stalls. The German plant physiologist Justus von Liebig called this 'the law of the minimum.' Modern greenhouse farmers in Pune use this to their advantage — they pump extra CO₂ into closed glasshouses (boosting concentration from atmospheric 0.04% to 0.1%) and see tomato yields jump 30%. They've identified CO₂ as the bottleneck and removed it. When you garden, watch for which factor is limiting yours — usually it's light in winter and water in summer.
deepDive.prerequisite: Tackle this after you're comfortable with the 4 conditions for photosynthesis (Class 7).
deepDive.nextStepHint: In Class 11 you'll see how each limiting factor affects a different enzyme in the Calvin cycle — that's why one limit slows the whole assembly line.

deepDive.title: Light reactions vs dark reactions — photosynthesis in two halves
deepDive.body: In Class 7 you wrote photosynthesis as: CO₂ + H₂O + light → glucose + O₂. Class 9 splits this single reaction into TWO stages happening in different parts of the chloroplast. STAGE 1 — light-dependent reactions: happen in the thylakoid membranes (those green stacks inside the chloroplast). Sunlight splits water into hydrogen + oxygen. The oxygen leaves; the hydrogen is captured in a molecule called NADPH. ATP is also made here. STAGE 2 — light-independent reactions (often misnamed 'dark reactions'): happen in the stroma (chloroplast's fluid). The captured hydrogen + ATP power a cycle that converts CO₂ into glucose. The first stage NEEDS light; the second only needs the products from the first stage. This is why a plant in darkness can briefly continue photosynthesis using stored NADPH — but only briefly.
deepDive.prerequisite: Tackle this after you're comfortable with the basic photosynthesis equation.
deepDive.nextStepHint: In Class 11 you'll meet the Calvin Cycle by name — three enzymes, three stages, the heart of the 'dark reactions'.

deepDive.title: C3 vs C4 vs CAM — three ways plants do photosynthesis
deepDive.body: In Class 7 photosynthesis was one process. In Class 11 you'll discover plants have evolved THREE different photosynthesis strategies. C3 plants (rice, wheat, most trees) — the original pathway. CO₂ is fixed into a 3-carbon molecule. Works great in moderate climates; loses ~30% of fixed CO₂ to a wasteful process called photorespiration in hot, dry conditions. C4 plants (sugarcane, maize, sorghum) — evolved 30 million years ago when atmospheric CO₂ dropped. They first concentrate CO₂ in special cells, THEN run C3. Twice as efficient in hot climates. That's why sugarcane outyields any other crop per hectare. CAM plants (pineapple, cactus, agave) — they open stomata only at night to grab CO₂, store it, then run photosynthesis with closed stomata in the day. Saves water dramatically. Indian farmers' choice of crop is, without knowing it, a choice between these three pathways.
deepDive.prerequisite: Tackle this after you're comfortable with light and dark reactions.
deepDive.nextStepHint: Modern agriculture is trying to engineer C4 traits into rice — a 'super rice' that could feed 50% more people from the same land.
